query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled alloying addition of silicon (in the range of 2–5 wt%) into boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion during hot-dip aluminum-plating.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components fabricated by conventional methods used for hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, without a silicon alloying modification.
generation.intervention: Incorporate 2–5 wt% silicon during the fabrication of the boride-based component.
generation.conditions: The intervention is evaluated under typical molten-aluminum exposure conditions in hot-dip plating, where the component is subjected to high-temperature aluminum contact.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of protective silicide phases or a silicide-enriched intermetallic/oxide interface that acts as a diffusion barrier to molten aluminum attack.
generation.mechanism: Silicon addition is expected to adjust the phase formation and diffusion behavior at the interface. The silicon promoted formation of silicide phases or modified oxide layers reduces the rate of aluminum dissolution and minimizes selective leaching of the boride, thereby enhancing corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to unalloyed boride components, the silicon-alloyed components will exhibit lower corrosion current densities, reduced mass loss, or a slower rate of structural degradation when exposed to molten aluminum.
generation.baseline: Performance of existing boride-based components without silicon addition under identical hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated only if the silicon content is optimized (2–5 wt%), as higher amounts could compromise the microstructure or mechanical properties. The effect will also depend on achieving uniform silicon distribution during fabrication.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the corrosion resistance improvement is uncertain and may vary with processing conditions and microstructural evolution; further study is required to quantify the improvement.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of boride-based samples: one set with a 2–5 wt% silicon addition and one control set without silicon. Subject both sets to the same hot-dip aluminum-plating process, ensuring identical thermal and environmental conditions. After exposure, assess the samples for corrosion damage.
measurements: Electrochemical corrosion current density (using Tafel analysis)
Surface morphology and phase composition analysis via SEM and XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the silicon-alloyed samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in corrosion resistance (i.e., lower mass loss, reduced corrosion current density, and formation of protective silicide/oxide phases) compared to the control samples under identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:4.1. Effect of Alloy Composition on Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior
cited_evidence.text: The chemical composition of an alloy determines the thermodynamic driving force for reaction between the molten salt and the alloy constituents []. Corrosion of an alloy in NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 molten salt is governed by the difference in Gibbs free energy of formation (ΔG°) for the salt constituents (NaCl, KCl, MgCl2) and corrosion products in the form of chlorides of the alloying elements (e.g., AlCl3, CrCl2, MnCl2, SiCl4, etc). Corrosion products with lower values of ΔG° are more likely to form and the associated alloying elements are likely to preferentially react with the salt and selectively leach out from the alloy. This leads to thermodynamic driving force for selective depletion of the alloying elements, i.e., dealloying at the surface [,].
